## At a glance

**Guiding question:** Are two measurement methods similar enough for this rehabilitation decision?\
**For:** physiotherapists, rehabilitation and trauma clinicians, and researchers who compare a new measurement method
with an established one. · **Prerequisites:** repeated measurements and the unit of analysis from @sec-b03; the
measurement chain from @sec-b10.\
**In the course:** [W4 · What imaging, gait and tissue models
measure](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w4-imaging-gait-tissue.html) (gait
station) and [W5 · Causal questions, trajectories and
phenotypes](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w5-causality-trajectories-phenotypes.html)
· **Data:** synthetic (generated in the chapter) · **Core reading time:** about 10 minutes

## Case and decision {#sec-b11-case}

A physiotherapist in a fictitious rehabilitation clinic follows patients after surgery for a tibial plateau fracture.
One criterion for moving a patient to the next stage of the gait programme is the peak knee flexion during the swing
phase. Until now it has been measured in the gait laboratory with a marker-based motion capture system, which is
booked out for weeks. A smartphone video analysed by a pose-estimation model would take five minutes on the ward. In
the first trial recordings the video values are systematically lower for some patients. Looking at the setup, the
physiotherapist notices that the phone stood at an angle to the walkway because the corridor is narrow. She has to
decide whether the video method may replace the laboratory measurement for this decision, and under which conditions.
The first error in this chapter is the perspective.

## Core reading {#sec-b11-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · recommended reading for W4 (gait station) · about 10 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

**From pixels to degrees.** A pose-estimation model is a learning model that finds anatomical landmarks in each video
frame, for example hip, knee and ankle, and returns their pixel coordinates with a confidence score
[@mathis2018deeplabcut]. Everything after that is geometry. The knee angle at one moment is the angle between the
thigh (knee to hip) and the shank (knee to ankle). Knee flexion is 180° minus that angle: 0° for a straight leg. Over
a gait cycle the flexion rises to a peak in the swing phase; that peak, in degrees, is the quantity the clinic wants.
@fig-b11-chain shows the whole chain and where the learning model sits.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b11-chain
#| fig-cap: "Measurement chain for knee flexion from video. The dashed box marks the learning model (pose estimation); the dark grey box marks the comparison with the reference method and the decision. Unit: degrees from step 5 onwards. Independent unit for the agreement question: patient (n = 24 in the lab, ten steps each). Synthetic case."
#| fig-alt: "Vertical flow chart with eight boxes: patient walking; camera position and frame rate; video frames in pixels; pose estimation of hip, knee and ankle (dashed box, learning model); knee angle from three points in degrees; peak flexion per step; mean per patient over ten steps; comparison with marker-based reference and rehabilitation decision. Notes on the right give the unit or reference for each step and state that the patient is the independent unit with n = 24."
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| code-fold: true
library(ggplot2)
# Generic drawing of a measurement chain: one box per step, a note per step, dashed border for the learning model
draw_chain <- function(steps, note_title = "Unit or reference") {
  steps$y <- rev(seq_len(nrow(steps)))
  types <- c("measurement", "reference", "model", "decision")
  ggplot(steps) +
    geom_segment(data = steps[-nrow(steps), ], aes(x = 1, xend = 1, y = y - 0.24, yend = y - 0.76),
                 arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(0.15, "cm")), colour = "grey30") +
    geom_tile(aes(x = 1, y = y, fill = type, linetype = type), width = 1.7, height = 0.5,
              colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(x = 1, y = y, label = label), size = 3.4) +
    geom_text(aes(x = 2.0, y = y, label = note), hjust = 0, size = 3.1, colour = "grey15") +
    annotate("text", x = 2.0, y = nrow(steps) + 0.55, label = note_title, hjust = 0, fontface = "bold",
             size = 3.2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(measurement = "white", reference = "grey85", model = "#D9ECF7",
                                 decision = "grey70"), breaks = types, name = NULL) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(measurement = "solid", reference = "solid", model = "dashed",
                                     decision = "solid"), breaks = types, name = NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.1, 4.6)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.5, nrow(steps) + 0.8)) +
    theme_void(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "#4D4D4D"))
}
chain_b11 <- data.frame(
  label = c("Patient walking", "Camera: position, frame rate", "Video frames", "Pose estimation",
            "Knee angle from 3 points", "Peak flexion per step", "Mean per patient", "Reference and decision"),
  note = c("knee flexion in the sagittal plane", "perpendicular to walkway? height? distance?",
           "pixels; face and body visible", "hip, knee, ankle in pixels + confidence",
           "degrees; 0 = straight leg", "degrees; 10 steps per patient", "independent unit: patient, n = 24",
           "marker-based motion capture; tolerance +/-5 degrees"),
  type = c("measurement", "measurement", "measurement", "model", "measurement", "measurement", "measurement",
           "decision")
)
draw_chain(chain_b11) +
  labs(caption = "Synthetic case · independent unit: patient (n = 24)")
```

```{r}
#| label: b11-geometry
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code: geometry for the perspective figure"
# Geometry used in the core reading (the lab explains the same functions step by step)
knee_flexion <- function(hip, knee, ankle) {
  hip <- matrix(hip, ncol = 2); knee <- matrix(knee, ncol = 2); ankle <- matrix(ankle, ncol = 2)
  v1 <- hip - knee; v2 <- ankle - knee
  cos_angle <- rowSums(v1 * v2) / sqrt(rowSums(v1^2) * rowSums(v2^2))
  180 - acos(pmin(pmax(cos_angle, -1), 1)) * 180 / pi
}
landmarks <- function(hip_flex, knee_flex, thigh = 0.43, shank = 0.42) {
  r <- pi / 180
  knee <- cbind(thigh * sin(hip_flex * r), -thigh * cos(hip_flex * r))
  ankle <- knee + cbind(shank * sin((hip_flex - knee_flex) * r), -shank * cos((hip_flex - knee_flex) * r))
  list(hip = cbind(0 * hip_flex, 0 * hip_flex), knee = knee, ankle = ankle)
}
project <- function(p, yaw) cbind(p[, 1] * cos(yaw * pi / 180), p[, 2])
seen <- function(knee_flex, yaw, hip_flex = 20) {
  L <- landmarks(hip_flex, knee_flex)
  knee_flexion(project(L$hip, yaw), project(L$knee, yaw), project(L$ankle, yaw))
}
proj_30_60 <- seen(60, 30)
```

**The perspective error.** A single camera sees a flat projection of a three-dimensional movement. If it looks at the
walkway at a right angle, the sagittal plane is projected without distortion. If the phone is turned by a yaw angle,
all forward-backward distances in the image shrink by the cosine of that angle while vertical distances stay. Thigh and
shank then look more vertical than they are, and the knee looks straighter. @fig-b11-perspective computes this for a
simplified setup without lens distortion: at a yaw of 30°, a true flexion of 60° appears as about
`r round(proj_30_60, 1)`°. The error is systematic, not random. Repeating the recording does not average it away, and
it is larger in patients who bend the knee more.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b11-perspective
#| fig-cap: "Systematic error of video-based knee flexion when the camera is turned away from the perpendicular, for true flexion of 40° and 60° (hip flexion 20°; simplified orthographic projection). Unit: degrees. Synthetic geometry, no patients involved."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart with camera yaw from 0 to 45 degrees on the horizontal axis and error in degrees (video minus true flexion) on the vertical axis. Both lines start at zero and fall with increasing yaw. The dashed line for 60 degrees true flexion falls faster, reaching about minus 6.5 degrees at 30 degrees yaw and about minus 15 degrees at 45 degrees yaw; the solid line for 40 degrees true flexion reaches about minus 5 degrees at 30 degrees yaw and about minus 11 degrees at 45 degrees yaw."
#| fig-height: 4
#| code-fold: true
grid_yaw <- expand.grid(yaw = 0:45, true_flexion = c(40, 60))
grid_yaw$error <- mapply(function(f, y) seen(f, y) - f, grid_yaw$true_flexion, grid_yaw$yaw)
grid_yaw$true_flexion <- factor(paste0(grid_yaw$true_flexion, "°"))
ggplot(grid_yaw, aes(yaw, error, linetype = true_flexion, colour = true_flexion)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-5, 0), colour = "grey50", linetype = c("dotted", "solid")) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = -5.6, label = "tolerance -5°", hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(cdsr_colours[c("blue", "red")])) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = cdsr_linetypes[1:2]) +
  labs(x = "Camera yaw relative to the perpendicular (degrees)", y = "Video minus true flexion (degrees)",
       colour = "True knee flexion", linetype = "True knee flexion",
       caption = "Synthetic geometry · thigh 0.43 m, shank 0.42 m · orthographic projection") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

**What the pose model knows.** The pose-estimation model was trained on labelled images, most of them of people in
everyday scenes. It has not necessarily seen crutches, knee braces, compression stockings or a far leg hidden behind the
near one (occlusion). Each of these can shift the knee landmark by a centimetre or two, and with a thigh of about
43 cm that already moves the angle by a few degrees. A low confidence score is a warning, not a correction. The model
is the only learned step in the chain; everything after it is geometry that can be checked by hand, as the lab does
with two angles worked out on paper.

**Reference and unit.** The comparison method is the laboratory's marker-based motion capture. It is itself a
measurement with its own error, not the truth, so an agreement study compares two methods and assumes neither to be
perfect. The physical unit is the degree throughout. The independent unit is the patient: 24 patients with ten steps
each in the lab.

**Agreement, not correlation.** To decide whether the video can replace the laboratory, the clinic records the same
steps with both methods and looks at the differences. The Bland–Altman approach plots the difference of the two methods
against their mean, estimates the average difference (bias) and the limits of agreement, within which about 95% of
differences are expected [@bland1986agreement]. A high correlation would say nothing useful: two methods can correlate
perfectly while one reads 10° lower. Details are in [Methods in R: Bland-Altman Limits of
Agreement](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-14-clinical.html#sec-chapters-14-clinical-bland-altman-analysis).

**Set the tolerance before looking.** Whether the limits of agreement are good enough is a clinical judgement, not a
statistical one, and it has to be made before the data are seen. In the fictitious protocol the progression criteria
are set in steps of 10°, so the team decides that a patient's value may differ from the laboratory value by at most
half a step. **The key assumption is a tolerance of ±5° for the value on which the decision is based** (*assumption*,
to be agreed locally). Published comparisons of two-dimensional video with motion capture report mean absolute
errors of several degrees for sagittal knee angles, so the question is realistic [@stenum2021gait; *published*].

**Which value is the decision based on?** Each patient contributes ten steps. Steps of the same patient are not
independent: they share the person, the camera setup and the clothing. The independent unit is the patient. Two
analyses are legitimate, and they answer different questions. If the decision uses a single step, the limits of
agreement must describe single steps; with repeated steps per patient they are estimated from the within-patient and
between-patient variance components [@bland2007multiple]. If the decision uses the mean of ten steps, the limits must
describe ten-step means, one per patient. Pooling all 240 steps as if they came from 240 patients is not legitimate: it
makes the uncertainty of the bias look smaller than it is. Which level applies, and how many steps a recording must
contain, is written into the protocol before the comparison starts.

**Question for the workshop:** Your clinic uses the mean of ten steps. Which of the two sets of limits of agreement
belongs in the clinical protocol, and what would have to change in the protocol if the ward only recorded three steps?

## Lab {#sec-b11-lab}

The lab simulates 24 fictitious patients with ten steps each, measured simultaneously by a marker-based reference and
by a video method whose landmarks carry noise and a small systematic offset. It then checks agreement at both decision
levels.

**Step 1 – the angle from three points.** The function accepts single points or one row per step and is checked
against two angles that can be worked out by hand.

```{r}
#| label: b11-angle
# Knee flexion in degrees from 2D hip, knee and ankle coordinates (x forward, z up); 0 = straight leg
knee_flexion <- function(hip, knee, ankle) {
  hip <- matrix(hip, ncol = 2); knee <- matrix(knee, ncol = 2); ankle <- matrix(ankle, ncol = 2)
  thigh_vec <- hip - knee                                   # from knee to hip
  shank_vec <- ankle - knee                                 # from knee to ankle
  cos_angle <- rowSums(thigh_vec * shank_vec) / sqrt(rowSums(thigh_vec^2) * rowSums(shank_vec^2))
  180 - acos(pmin(pmax(cos_angle, -1), 1)) * 180 / pi       # flexion = 180 degrees minus the inner angle
}
stopifnot(
  abs(knee_flexion(c(0, 0), c(0, -1), c(0, -2)) - 0) < 1e-9,    # straight leg: 0 degrees
  abs(knee_flexion(c(0, 0), c(0, -1), c(-1, -1)) - 90) < 1e-9   # shank horizontal: 90 degrees
)
knee_flexion(c(0, 0), c(0.15, -0.40), c(-0.20, -0.65))          # an arbitrary example in metres
```

**Step 2 – synthetic patients and steps.** Landmarks are generated in the sagittal plane, projected for the camera's
yaw, offset and blurred like a pose-estimation output, and then turned back into angles.

```{r}
#| label: b11-simulate
set.seed(1111)
n_patients <- 24
n_steps <- 10
patients <- data.frame(
  patient = sprintf("P%02d", 1:n_patients),
  mean_flexion = rnorm(n_patients, 55, 7),    # true peak swing flexion per patient (degrees)
  hip_flexion = rnorm(n_patients, 20, 3),     # hip flexion at that moment (degrees)
  yaw = runif(n_patients, -5, 5),             # camera almost perpendicular (degrees)
  knee_offset = rnorm(n_patients, 0.004, 0.006), # knee landmark placed slightly anterior (metres)
  size = rnorm(n_patients, 1, 0.05)           # body size factor for segment lengths
)
# Landmarks in metres for given hip and knee flexion; projection for a camera turned by 'yaw' degrees
landmarks <- function(hip_flex, knee_flex, thigh = 0.43, shank = 0.42) {
  r <- pi / 180
  knee <- cbind(thigh * sin(hip_flex * r), -thigh * cos(hip_flex * r))
  ankle <- knee + cbind(shank * sin((hip_flex - knee_flex) * r), -shank * cos((hip_flex - knee_flex) * r))
  list(hip = cbind(0 * hip_flex, 0 * hip_flex), knee = knee, ankle = ankle)
}
project <- function(p, yaw) cbind(p[, 1] * cos(yaw * pi / 180), p[, 2])
simulate_steps <- function(patients, yaw) {
  rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(patients)), function(i) {
    true <- patients$mean_flexion[i] + rnorm(n_steps, 0, 2.5)        # step-to-step variation
    hip <- patients$hip_flexion[i] + rnorm(n_steps, 0, 2)
    L <- landmarks(hip, true, 0.43 * patients$size[i], 0.42 * patients$size[i])
    L$knee[, 1] <- L$knee[, 1] + patients$knee_offset[i]               # systematic landmark offset
    blur <- function() matrix(rnorm(2 * n_steps, 0, 0.012), ncol = 2)  # landmark noise, metres
    video <- knee_flexion(project(L$hip, yaw[i]) + blur(), project(L$knee, yaw[i]) + blur(),
                          project(L$ankle, yaw[i]) + blur())
    data.frame(patient = patients$patient[i], step = 1:n_steps, true = true,
               reference = true + rnorm(n_steps, 0, 1),               # marker-based reference
               video = video)
  })
  steps <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  steps$difference <- steps$video - steps$reference
  steps
}
steps <- simulate_steps(patients, patients$yaw)
gait_file <- steps[, c("patient", "step", "reference", "video")]
gait_file[, c("reference", "video")] <- round(gait_file[, c("reference", "video")], 2)   # degrees, 2 decimals
write.csv(gait_file, "../data/b11-gait-steps.csv", row.names = FALSE)
c(patients = length(unique(steps$patient)), steps = nrow(steps))
```

The file [`data/b11-gait-steps.csv`](../data/b11-gait-steps.csv) holds the synthetic reference and video values for
the gait station in W4; the true values stay in the simulation.

**Step 3 – agreement at both decision levels.** The single-step limits use the variance components of Bland and
Altman's method for repeated measurements in which the true value varies [@bland2007multiple]. The ten-step limits use
one mean difference per patient.

```{r}
#| label: b11-agreement
tolerance <- 5                                     # degrees, set before the analysis (assumption)
# (a) Single steps: one-way ANOVA of the differences by patient
fit <- anova(lm(difference ~ patient, data = steps))
ms_within <- fit["Residuals", "Mean Sq"]
ms_between <- fit["patient", "Mean Sq"]
var_between <- max(0, (ms_between - ms_within) / n_steps)
bias <- mean(steps$difference)
sd_single <- sqrt(var_between + ms_within)
# (b) Ten-step means: one value per patient
per_patient <- aggregate(cbind(reference, video, difference) ~ patient, data = steps, FUN = mean)
sd_mean10 <- sd(per_patient$difference)
# Confidence interval of the bias: patients are the independent unit (n = 24), not steps (n = 240)
ci_patients <- bias + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, n_patients - 1) * sd_mean10 / sqrt(n_patients)
ci_steps_wrong <- bias + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, nrow(steps) - 1) * sd(steps$difference) / sqrt(nrow(steps))
agreement <- data.frame(
  decision_level = c("single step", "mean of 10 steps"),
  bias = bias, lower_loa = bias - 1.96 * c(sd_single, sd_mean10), upper_loa = bias + 1.96 * c(sd_single, sd_mean10)
)
agreement$within_tolerance <- agreement$lower_loa >= -tolerance & agreement$upper_loa <= tolerance
agreement
rbind(ci_bias_patients = ci_patients, ci_bias_steps_wrong = ci_steps_wrong)
stopifnot(agreement$within_tolerance == c(FALSE, TRUE),
          diff(ci_patients) > diff(ci_steps_wrong))      # pooling steps understates the uncertainty
```

For single steps the limits of agreement run from `r round(agreement$lower_loa[1], 1)`° to
`r round(agreement$upper_loa[1], 1)`° and exceed the tolerance. For the ten-step mean they run from
`r round(agreement$lower_loa[2], 1)`° to `r round(agreement$upper_loa[2], 1)`° and lie within it. The video method,
recorded perpendicular to the walkway, is acceptable for a decision based on ten steps and not for one based on a
single step. The confidence interval for the bias based on 24 patients
(`r round(ci_patients[1], 1)`° to `r round(ci_patients[2], 1)`°) is wider than the one obtained by pretending that
240 steps were 240 patients (`r round(ci_steps_wrong[1], 1)`° to `r round(ci_steps_wrong[2], 1)`°).

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Averaging the ten steps per patient first and then quoting the resulting limits of agreement as if they applied to
single measurements. Limits of agreement belong to the quantity on which they were computed: limits for ten-step means
are narrower than limits for single steps and must not be used for a protocol that relies on one step.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-b11-ba
#| fig-cap: "Bland–Altman plot for peak knee flexion, video minus marker-based reference, in degrees. Large symbols: ten-step means per patient (n = 24 independent patients); small grey dots: single steps (240). Solid line: bias; dashed lines: limits of agreement for ten-step means; dotted lines: limits for single steps; shaded band: pre-specified tolerance of ±5° (assumption). Synthetic data."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot with the mean of both methods (about 30 to 72 degrees) on the horizontal axis and the difference video minus reference on the vertical axis (about minus 8 to plus 11 degrees). A grey band marks plus and minus 5 degrees. Twenty-four large points for patient means lie close to a bias line of about plus 1 degree, all within the band, with dashed limits at about minus 1.5 and plus 4 degrees. Two hundred and forty small grey points for single steps scatter more widely; the dotted single-step limits at about minus 6 and plus 8.6 degrees lie outside the band."
#| code-fold: true
steps$mean_methods <- (steps$video + steps$reference) / 2
per_patient$mean_methods <- (per_patient$video + per_patient$reference) / 2
lines_ba <- data.frame(y = c(bias, agreement$lower_loa[2], agreement$upper_loa[2], agreement$lower_loa[1],
                             agreement$upper_loa[1]),
                       type = c("bias", "limits, 10-step mean", "limits, 10-step mean", "limits, single step",
                                "limits, single step"))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -tolerance, ymax = tolerance, fill = "grey90") +
  geom_point(data = steps, aes(mean_methods, difference), colour = "grey55", size = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = per_patient, aes(mean_methods, difference), colour = cdsr_colours["blue"], size = 2.8,
             shape = cdsr_shapes[1]) +
  geom_hline(data = lines_ba, aes(yintercept = y, linetype = type)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("bias" = "solid", "limits, 10-step mean" = "dashed",
                                   "limits, single step" = "dotted"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Mean of video and reference (degrees)", y = "Video minus reference (degrees)",
       caption = "Synthetic data · n = 24 patients, 10 steps each · tolerance ±5° (assumption)") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Other implementation: Python with PyTorch"}
Pose estimation itself is rarely written in R. The PyTorch library torchvision offers a [Keypoint R-CNN
model](https://docs.pytorch.org/vision/stable/models/keypoint_rcnn.html) with weights trained on the COCO person
keypoints (`KeypointRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_Weights.COCO_V1`), which returns 17 keypoints per person, including both hips,
knees and ankles, as `[x, y, visibility]` in pixel coordinates; inputs are expected as tensors scaled to the range
0–1 [@paszke2019pytorch]. For landmarks that COCO does not define, such as markers on a brace, DeepLabCut trains a
network on a few hundred hand-labelled frames [@mathis2018deeplabcut]. The concrete advantage is a tested detector
with known weights instead of hand-placed points. To compare it fairly with this lab, the following must be identical
and recorded: the video frames (frame rate, resolution and the phone's rotation metadata), the mapping from keypoint
index to hip, knee and ankle of the correct side, the handling of low-confidence keypoints, the definition of a step
and its peak, the averaging over ten steps, the metric (difference to the reference in degrees) and the tolerance of
±5°. Weights and software version (torchvision 0.29.2 or DeepLabCut 3.0.2 in November 2026) belong in the model
passport. Status: conceptual comparison, not run.
:::

## Counter-check {#sec-b11-countercheck}

Now reproduce the error from the case. For the first eight patients the phone stands at 30° to the walkway; the
remaining sixteen are recorded as before. Predict first: does the bias move up or down, and do the ten-step limits of
agreement stay within ±5°?

```{r}
#| label: b11-countercheck
set.seed(2111)
yaw_corridor <- patients$yaw
yaw_corridor[1:8] <- 30                             # narrow corridor: camera turned by 30 degrees
steps_corridor <- simulate_steps(patients, yaw_corridor)
pp_corridor <- aggregate(difference ~ patient, data = steps_corridor, FUN = mean)
pp_corridor$setup <- ifelse(pp_corridor$patient %in% patients$patient[1:8], "turned 30 degrees", "perpendicular")
bias_by_setup <- tapply(pp_corridor$difference, pp_corridor$setup, mean)
loa_corridor <- mean(pp_corridor$difference) + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sd(pp_corridor$difference)
round(c(bias_by_setup, lower_loa = loa_corridor[1], upper_loa = loa_corridor[2]), 1)
stopifnot(bias_by_setup["turned 30 degrees"] < bias_by_setup["perpendicular"] - 3,
          loa_corridor[1] < -tolerance)
```

The bias in the turned setup is `r round(bias_by_setup["turned 30 degrees"], 1)`° against
`r round(bias_by_setup["perpendicular"], 1)`° with a perpendicular camera, and the lower limit of agreement of the
ten-step means falls to `r round(loa_corridor[1], 1)`°, outside the tolerance. The perspective error is systematic, so
averaging steps does not remove it. The plausible failure mode is therefore concrete: *a phone placed at an angle
underestimates knee flexion, most in patients with the largest flexion, and may hold patients back in the programme*.
The checkable measurement assumption is equally concrete: *the camera axis is perpendicular to the walkway within
±10°, verified with a floor marking and a photo of the setup for every recording*.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b11-consequences}

**An identifiable movement pattern.** A gait video shows face, body and clothing, and it is health data. Removing the
face is not enough: gait patterns are so individual that learning models can attribute them to single persons from
joint angles and forces alone [@horst2019gait; *published*]. The derived keypoint trajectories may therefore still
identify a patient, especially combined with ward and date. The General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) defines biometric
data as personal data resulting from specific technical processing of physical, physiological or behavioural
characteristics "which allow or confirm the unique identification" of a person (Article 4(14)); Article 9(1) lists
biometric data "for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person" and data concerning health among the special
categories [@eu2016dsgvo; binding text]. Whether the keypoint data in this case fall under the biometric category is a
question of interpretation for the data protection officer; that in this clinical context they are data concerning
health (Article 4(15)) is hardly in doubt. The decision
the team has to take is practical: does the clinic need the raw video for its purpose, for example to audit
implausible angles, and if so, for how long? @sec-b23 follows exactly this data flow from video to angle and
deletion point.

**Regulation.** If the clinic used the app's output to decide a patient's progression, the intended purpose stated by
the manufacturer would determine whether the software is a medical device and of which class (Rule 11 of Annex VIII of
the MDR [@eu2017mdr]). An app marketed for "fitness tracking" and used for a clinical decision raises its own
question. @sec-b22 works through such intended purposes.

**Ethics and operations.** A systematic underestimation does not hit everyone alike: it is largest in patients with
the largest flexion and in wards with the narrowest corridors. The patient sees only "not yet". A short note in the
protocol on camera setup, and a re-measurement in the laboratory when the video value lies within 5° of a decision
threshold, keep the faster method without shifting its errors onto patients.

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b11-lookup}

- **Reviewer question:** The study reports limits of agreement of ±4° from 600 steps of 30 participants. Were the
  limits computed for single steps or for participant means, how were repeated steps handled, and was the tolerance
  defined before the analysis?
- **Self-test:** The ward wants to record only three steps per patient. Using the variance components from the lab,
  estimate the limits of agreement for a three-step mean. Is the video method still acceptable at a tolerance of ±5°?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
```{r}
#| label: b11-selftest
#| echo: false
loa_3 <- bias + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sqrt(var_between + ms_within / 3)   # limits for a three-step mean
stopifnot(loa_3[2] > tolerance)
```

For the mean of $m$ steps the variance of a patient's mean difference is the between-patient component plus the
within-patient component divided by $m$. With the lab's values (between-patient variance
`r round(var_between, 2)`, within-patient variance `r round(ms_within, 2)`, both in squared degrees) a three-step mean
has a standard deviation of `r round(sqrt(var_between + ms_within / 3), 2)`° and limits of agreement from
`r round(bias - 1.96 * sqrt(var_between + ms_within / 3), 1)`° to
`r round(bias + 1.96 * sqrt(var_between + ms_within / 3), 1)`°. In R:
`bias + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sqrt(var_between + ms_within / 3)`. The upper limit exceeds +5°, so at this tolerance the
video method is not acceptable for a three-step protocol, although it is for ten steps. A protocol based on three
steps needs its own agreement statement and must not reuse the ten-step limits. The estimate also assumes that three steps on the ward vary like ten steps in the laboratory, which itself is
an assumption to check.
:::

- **Annotated sources:**
  - @bland1986agreement introduced limits of agreement and explains why correlation is the wrong tool.
  - @bland2007multiple provides the variance-components method for several observations per person used in the lab.
  - @stenum2021gait compares two-dimensional video pose estimation with motion capture on a stride-by-stride basis and
    shows realistic error sizes for sagittal knee angles.
  - @mathis2018deeplabcut describes markerless pose estimation of user-defined landmarks with a learning model.
  - @horst2019gait supports the statement that individual gait patterns are distinctive enough to identify people.
  - @eu2016dsgvo is the binding text for the definitions of biometric and health data.
